name: Cree, west coast of James Bay
confidence_why: Ellis 1983, the principal describer of the dialect, says stress on the west coast of James Bay is non-distinctive and marks its degrees only as an aid to memory, and Cook 1991, who quotes him verbatim and read his marked text, calls the placement unpredictable though often antepenultimate, so no placement rule can be stated for Moose Cree; the record rests on that one source, known through Cook's…

catalog_quote: Ellis, describing the dialect of Cree spoken on the west coast of James Bay, says: In Cree, stress is non-distinctive: i.e., it never keeps two otherwise identical words apart as in the case of English, pérmit — noun, versus permít — verb. There are, however, clearly marked degrees of stress; and for the first unit in particular, and for longer utterances, these have been marked as an aid to memory: (´) is used to show the strongest stress on a word or phrase. (ˋ) is used to mark the next to strongest. (Ellis 1983:36) From the stress marked by Ellis in the text on page 71, stress is indeed unpredictable, although the strongest stress is quite frequently on the antepenultimate syllable. However, one has to remember that what Ellis deals with is textual material, not individual lexical items.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ellis states no positional rule: stress is non-distinctive, but audible degrees of stress exist and are marked in the pedagogical text (strongest and next-strongest) as a memory aid, i.e. presented as something to be learned per utterance rather than derived. Cook's reading of Ellis's marked text is that placement is unpredictable, with the strongest stress most often on the antepenultimate syllable. (Cook's own antepenultimate-stress rule, with penult surface cases from i-deletion, is argued on Plains Cree data, not Moose Cree.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Ellis marks a 'next to strongest' degree with a second diacritic in the marked texts; no rule for its placement is stated. Cook marks only the strongest stress and says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated by Ellis; Cook: 'stress is indeed unpredictable, although the strongest stress is quite frequently on the antepenultimate syllable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Ellis's marking is on 'a word or phrase' within units and 'longer utterances' of a spoken-language course, i.e. connected speech, not citation forms; Cook explicitly notes 'what Ellis deals with is textual material, not individual lexical items'. The statement covers the composite west-coast-of-James-Bay variety (Moose Factory l-dialect plus Fort Albany n-dialect), not Moose Cree alone.
new_statements.identity_note: The only located stress statement is Ellis's, for 'the dialect of Cree spoken on the west coast of James Bay'. Ellis's Spoken Cree (1962/1983/2000) is a composite of the l-dialect of Moose Factory (= Moose Cree, moos1236) and the n-dialect of Fort Albany/Kashechewan (= Swampy Cree, swam1239); Wolfart 1973: fn. 10 says 'in Ellis, 1962 the text shows l' (i.e. the printed forms are Moose Cree), and Ellis 1995 (Introduction p. xiii) defines Moose Cree as the l-dialect of Moose Factory, Swampy Cree as the n-dialect north of Moosonee, and 'Kashechewan Cree' as a mixed n-l usage. The same Ellis 1983:36 statement is already the pending works still to obtain for swam1239, so the two records would rest on one source. Cook 1991's own data (antepenultimate rule) are Plains Cree from northern Alberta (plai1258), not Moose Cree.
